# Hosted topology

How a running instance of Buzz -- the relay and its companion services -- is laid out
across execution nodes, which containers/services map to which data stores, where the
network, persistence and trust boundaries sit, and what deployment automation is
authoritative for each of those. This node covers the deployment topology that is
actually inspectable from this repository: the OSS Helm chart under
`deploy/charts/`. It is the same shape of artifact (a Helm chart, deployed by ArgoCD to
a Kubernetes cluster) that top-level `AGENTS.md`'s ecosystem table says
`squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks` uses for Block's own staging deployment -- see
*Scope and omissions* for exactly what that connection does and does not establish.

## Environment and execution nodes

The execution node is a **Kubernetes cluster**. The chart targets two profiles selected
by chart values, not by a separate codebase:

- **Production** — external managed Postgres, Redis and S3-compatible storage; secrets
  supplied via a pre-created Kubernetes `Secret` (`secrets.existingSecret`); no
  chart-side secret generation; horizontally scalable (`replicaCount >= 2`, requires
  Redis). Deployed via ArgoCD or Flux, both of which render the chart with
  `helm template`.
- **Quickstart** — single-node evaluation only. Postgres, Redis and MinIO are bundled
  in-cluster as chart-managed subcharts/Deployments, and the chart autogenerates its own
  relay and service secrets. Not GitOps-safe and not intended to carry production
  traffic.

Two independent Helm charts exist, each its own release lifecycle and each published to
`oci://ghcr.io/block/buzz/charts/…`:

- `deploy/charts/buzz` — the relay, its optional device-pairing relay, and all
  relay-adjacent Kubernetes resources.
- `deploy/charts/buzz-push-gateway` — Buzz's APNs last-hop push-delivery gateway, a
  separate Deployment with its own dedicated database.

## Containers, services and data stores

| Component | What it is | Backing store(s) |
|---|---|---|
| `relay` container (Deployment) | Single `buzz-relay` binary: WebSocket + REST + web UI + git smart-HTTP + huddle audio, all in one process | PostgreSQL (event store, migrated via embedded `sqlx::migrate!`), Redis (`buzz-pubsub` fan-out, required once `replicaCount > 1`), S3-compatible object storage (media + git pack objects) |
| `relay` Service (ClusterIP) | Fronts the relay container's three named ports: `app` (3000 — WS/REST/web UI), `health` (8080), `metrics` (9102) | — |
| `git-repos` volume | Per-pod working-tree cache for the relay's git endpoint | `PersistentVolumeClaim` (ReadWriteOnce) when `persistence.git.enabled`, else an ephemeral `emptyDir` |
| `git-pack-cache` volume | Process-local immutable pack/index cache | Always an `emptyDir` |
| `buzz-pair-relay` container (optional Deployment) | Stateless device-pairing WebSocket relay, same image, different entrypoint | None — genuinely stateless |
| `buzz-push-gateway` (separate chart, Deployment) | APNs last-hop push delivery | Its own dedicated PostgreSQL database, reached over a network-policy-restricted CIDR list |

Object storage (S3-compatible: bundled MinIO in Quickstart, or an external provider in
Production) is the one store shared between two responsibilities — media blobs and git
pack objects — distinguished by key prefix/bucket layout rather than by separate
services. Full-text search runs inside PostgreSQL; the chart provisions no separate
search service.

## Network boundaries

- The relay `Service` is `ClusterIP` by default and is not itself a public network
  boundary.
- Public ingress is **optional and pluggable**: the chart can render either a
  Kubernetes `Ingress` (`networking.k8s.io/v1`) or a Gateway API `HTTPRoute`, neither
  enabled unless the operator opts in, both routing to the same Service ports.
- The maintained GitOps examples terminate TLS at an `nginx` `IngressClass` with
  cert-manager, and explicitly raise `proxy-read-timeout`/`proxy-send-timeout` to
  3600s — because the relay's primary protocol is a long-lived WebSocket connection,
  not short HTTP request/response.
- The device-pairing relay gets no chart-managed Ingress/HTTPRoute at all; an operator
  routes its own public hostname straight to the pairing Service.
- `buzz-push-gateway` draws its network boundary the tightest of any component here: a
  `NetworkPolicy` whitelists only DNS egress, an operator-named APNs CIDR list on 443,
  and an operator-named Postgres CIDR list on 5432, and the chart *fails to render*
  rather than default its metrics-scrape ingress open — an explicit fail-closed choice
  in the template itself.

## Persistence boundaries

Two different persistence models coexist in the same deployment:

- **Event and metadata state (PostgreSQL)** is the single canonical event store and is
  authoritative — losing it is losing history. Migrations are embedded in the relay
  binary and race-safe across replicas via a Postgres advisory lock.
- **Git object/ref state is not authoritative on any pod-local filesystem.** Every git
  request hydrates an ephemeral working tree from a manifest published to
  S3-compatible object storage, so the relay is "multi-instance-ready by construction"
  — nothing on local disk needs cross-instance coordination. This is why each replica
  needs only a `ReadWriteOnce` volume (or none at all) rather than a shared
  `ReadWriteMany` filesystem, and why losing a pod's `git-repos` PVC or its
  `git-pack-cache` causes no data loss, only a slower next hydrate.
- **Media blobs** live in the same S3-compatible bucket, addressed either `path`- or
  `virtual`-style depending on the provider.

## Trust boundaries (secrets)

No secret value is described by content here — only how each one flows.

- Every credential the relay container consumes (relay private key, git-hook HMAC
  secret, database URLs, Redis URL, S3 access/secret keys) reaches the container
  exclusively through Kubernetes `Secret` key references on the container spec, several
  marked `optional: true` so an absent key degrades a feature instead of blocking the
  rollout. None is ever a plaintext pod environment literal.
- The chart *can* generate its own Secret, but that path is explicitly documented as
  not GitOps-safe (its random-value generation is non-idempotent under the
  `helm template` rendering both ArgoCD and Flux use), and both maintained GitOps
  examples set `secrets.existingSecret` instead. Production trust boundary: an
  externally managed Secret (SealedSecrets, SOPS, External Secrets, or Vault, per the
  chart's own sample), never chart-side generation.
- `buzz-push-gateway` separates its migration trust boundary from its serving trust
  boundary: the migration Job holds DDL-capable credentials, while the runtime
  `DATABASE_URL` is documented as scoped to a role with only `CONNECT` plus DML on the
  gateway's six tables.

## Deployment automation and configuration as authority

These are the files this node summarizes and defers to — where they and this document
disagree, they win:

| For | Read |
|---|---|
| The relay + pairing-relay chart itself | `deploy/charts/buzz/` (`values.yaml`, `values.schema.json`, `templates/`) |
| Narrative walkthrough, profiles, HA rules, S3 addressing, upgrades, backups | `deploy/charts/buzz/README.md` |
| A canonical ArgoCD install | `deploy/charts/buzz/examples/argocd-app.yaml` |
| A canonical Flux install | `deploy/charts/buzz/examples/flux-helmrelease.yaml` |
| The existing-Secret schema production deployments must supply | `deploy/charts/buzz/examples/secret-sample.yaml` |
| The push-gateway chart | `deploy/charts/buzz-push-gateway/` |
| The formal safety argument behind object-storage-backed git | `docs/git-on-object-storage.md` |
| Which repos build and ship what, including Block's internal staging pipeline | `AGENTS.md` § Ecosystem |
| The Compose-based (non-Kubernetes) local/self-host alternative | `deploy/compose/` |

## Failure and recovery implications

- **Rolling updates are zero-unavailability by chart design**: `RollingUpdate` with
  `maxSurge: 1`, `maxUnavailable: 0`.
- **A relay pod's local disk state is disposable.** The only state a lost pod cannot
  regenerate by itself is the state enumerated in the chart's own backup list: the
  relay private key (rotating it changes the relay's federation identity), the
  PostgreSQL database, the S3 bucket, the `git` PVC (recoverable slowly by re-hydrating
  from object storage, per the persistence-boundary section above), and the owner's
  private key (held by the operator, not the chart — recovered by reinstalling with the
  same `ownerPubkey`).
- **Readiness is coupled to object-storage reachability.** With the relay's S3
  conformance probe at its default (enabled), a probe failure is startup-fatal and
  `/_readiness` never opens — an operator who disables that probe trades an early,
  clear failure signal for a later one on the first real storage operation.
  Independent of that probe, the chart's readiness check only verifies **database
  connectivity, never schema freshness** — an operator who decouples migrations
  (`migrate.autoMigrate=false`) and forgets to run `buzz-admin migrate` gets pods that
  report healthy while serving against a stale schema.
- **`replicaCount > 1` is an all-or-nothing invariant, not a soft recommendation.**
  Redis becomes mandatory the moment a second replica is requested, and the chart
  refuses to render (rather than silently running a partitioned deployment) if that
  isn't satisfied.
- **Autoscaling and disruption budgets are opt-in levers, not defaults.** An operator
  who wants pod-loss tolerance under voluntary disruption must enable the
  `PodDisruptionBudget` explicitly; it only renders once the effective minimum replica
  count is greater than 1.
- **`buzz-push-gateway`'s failure/recovery surface is narrower and separately owned**:
  its dedicated database and DDL/DML credential split mean a push-gateway incident does
  not, by the topology described here, touch the relay's own database or its
  credentials.

## Scope and omissions

**This document covers** the Kubernetes-based hosted deployment topology of Buzz as
expressed by the two OSS Helm charts in this repository (`deploy/charts/buzz` and
`deploy/charts/buzz-push-gateway`): execution nodes, the container/service/data-store
mapping, network/persistence/trust boundaries, the deployment automation that is
authoritative, and the failure/recovery implications those files document.

**It does not cover, and these are gaps rather than silence:**

| Not covered here | Owned by |
|---|---|
| `squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks`'s actual Terraform and ArgoCD configuration for Block's staging cluster — a private repository outside this checkout, never opened for this node | that repository |
| `squareup/sprout-oss`'s CI pipeline building the relay Docker image and pushing to internal ECR — also outside this checkout | that repository |
| The Compose-based (non-Kubernetes) deployment path at `deploy/compose/`, an alternative topology for operators who are not running Kubernetes | a future corpus node, not this one |
| Per-type corpus templates, and the field-combination matrix and enum members themselves | `launchpad/docs/corpus/schema/node.schema.json`, per `launchpad/docs/corpus/AGENTS.md` |
| The relay's internal request-handling architecture (subsystems, event flow inside one pod) | a future `architecture` corpus node on the relay's internal layout, not this deployment-topology node |

**Expected but not verified when this node was written:**

- **Whether `block-coder-tf-stacks` deploys `deploy/charts/buzz` specifically, versus a
  fork, an older pinned version, or a values overlay this repository does not carry.**
  `AGENTS.md`'s ecosystem diagram names the deployed artifact "Helm chart -> ArgoCD ->
  staging cluster," which matches this chart's own shape, but that repository was not
  opened for this node — the connection above is recorded as an `INFERENCE`, not a
  `FACT`, for exactly that reason.
- **Whether Block's staging cluster runs the Production profile as described here**
  (external managed Postgres/Redis/S3, `existingSecret`) rather than some
  staging-specific variant. Not verifiable from this checkout.
- **Runtime behavior under an actual node/zone failure** (as opposed to a voluntary
  `kubectl drain` the PodDisruptionBudget governs) was not exercised; the failure modes
  above are documented ones, not observed ones.

evidence.statement: This node was authored and checked against repository revision a44cf52fc740ebebbdd671427480d14f0bce0115.
Buzz's hosted deployment is a single relay binary serving WebSocket + REST + the web UI, backed by PostgreSQL, Redis, and S3-compatible object storage.

The relay binary is built from the buzz-relay crate (bin name buzz-relay, entry point crates/buzz-relay/src/main.rs), described in its own manifest as the WebSocket relay server for the Buzz communications platform, and is published independently of the desktop/mobile version.

Block's own hosted (staging) deployment of Buzz is produced by a repo pipeline distinct from this one: squareup/sprout-oss builds the relay Docker image and pushes it to internal ECR, and squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks applies Terraform to run ArgoCD, which deploys a Helm chart to the staging Kubernetes cluster.

The Helm chart at deploy/charts/buzz is the OSS chart published to ghcr.io/block/buzz/charts/buzz, designed for ArgoCD and Flux GitOps sync (both render via `helm template`), with two operating profiles: Production (external managed Postgres/Redis/S3, `secrets.existingSecret`, no chart-side secret autogeneration, HA-capable at `replicaCount >= 2`) and Quickstart (in-cluster Postgres+Redis+MinIO bundled in, chart-autogenerated secrets, single replica, eval-only).

AGENTS.md's own ecosystem diagram names the artifact block-coder-tf-stacks deploys as "Helm chart -> ArgoCD -> staging cluster", which is the same shape (Helm chart, ArgoCD) documented independently in deploy/charts/buzz/README.md and its examples/argocd-app.yaml -- consistent with, though not proof of, block-coder-tf-stacks deploying this chart specifically.

The relay Deployment's container exposes three named ports on the pod (app 3000, health 8080, metrics 9102 by default) and mounts two volumes: a git-repos volume that is a PersistentVolumeClaim when persistence.git.enabled is true (else an ephemeral emptyDir), and a git-pack-cache emptyDir.
A Service of type ClusterIP fronts the relay Deployment's three ports (app/health/metrics), matched by pod selector; the chart does not itself terminate a public network boundary at this Service.
replicaCount > 1 hard-requires Redis (for buzz-pubsub fan-out); the chart template-fails at render time if that invariant is broken, rather than silently degrading to a partitioned deployment.

Git repository ref and object state is not authoritative on any pod-local filesystem: every git request hydrates an ephemeral working tree from a manifest published to S3-compatible object storage, the write path additionally returns the parent state its compare-and-swap predicates on, and the relay is stated to be multi-instance-ready by construction because nothing on local disk needs to be coordinated between instances.

Because git state is object-store-backed rather than filesystem-authoritative, each relay replica needs only its own ReadWriteOnce PersistentVolumeClaim (no ReadWriteMany/shared filesystem); the chart's pvc-git.yaml template creates one such PVC per release when persistence.git.enabled is true and no existingClaim is supplied, and repo-name uniqueness is kept in Postgres rather than on that volume.

Losing a relay pod's local git-pack-cache (always an emptyDir) or even its git-repos PersistentVolumeClaim causes no data loss, only reduced hydrate performance until the cache repopulates from object storage on the next request.

Public network ingress to the relay Service is optional and pluggable rather than chart-mandated: the chart conditionally renders either a Kubernetes Ingress (networking.k8s.io/v1) or a Gateway API HTTPRoute, both disabled unless explicitly enabled, targeting the same Service ports.

The maintained ArgoCD/Flux examples front the relay with an nginx IngressClass, cert-manager-issued TLS, and WebSocket-friendly proxy timeouts (proxy-read-timeout and proxy-send-timeout raised to 3600s) -- because the relay's primary protocol is a long-lived WebSocket connection, not request/response HTTP.

Buzz's device-pairing relay (a separate stateless WebSocket binary, buzz-pair-relay, reusing the same container image) can run as its own optional Deployment and ClusterIP-configurable Service; the chart creates no Ingress/HTTPRoute for it, leaving the operator to route its own public hostname directly to the pairing Service.

Production secrets (BUZZ_RELAY_PRIVATE_KEY, BUZZ_GIT_HOOK_HMAC_SECRET, DATABASE_URL, READ_DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, BUZZ_S3_ACCESS_KEY, BUZZ_S3_SECRET_KEY) reach the relay container only via Kubernetes Secret key references, several of them marked optional so an unset key degrades a feature rather than failing the whole rollout; no secret value is ever rendered as a plain pod environment literal by the chart.

The chart's own Secret template only renders when secrets.existingSecret is unset, is explicitly documented as not GitOps-safe (its randAlphaNum-based generation is non-idempotent under `helm template`, which is how ArgoCD and Flux both render), and both maintained GitOps examples set secrets.existingSecret instead of relying on it.

The documented schema for that existingSecret names every key it may carry (relay identity, HMAC secret, database and cache URLs, object-storage credentials) and instructs the operator to manage it with an external-secrets tool -- SealedSecrets, SOPS, External Secrets, or Vault -- specifically so the unencrypted values never enter the Git repository GitOps syncs from.

A second, independently versioned Helm chart, buzz-push-gateway, hosts Buzz's APNs last-hop push-delivery capability as its own Deployment with its own dedicated database, published separately to the same GHCR OCI registry as the relay chart.

buzz-push-gateway enforces its network trust boundary with a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that restricts pod egress to DNS, an operator-supplied list of APNs CIDR blocks on port 443, and an operator-supplied list of Postgres CIDR blocks on port 5432, and only opens ingress on its private metrics port to a namespace/pod selector the operator names explicitly -- the chart's own template fails to render rather than default that scrape ingress open.

buzz-push-gateway's schema migrations run under DDL-capable credentials that are distinct from its runtime DATABASE_URL, which is documented as scoped to a dedicated role holding only CONNECT plus DML on the gateway's six tables -- separating the migration trust boundary from the request-serving one.

Relay readiness is coupled to object-storage reachability by default: when the relay's S3 conformance probe is enabled (the relay's own default), a probe failure at startup is fatal and the pod's /_readiness endpoint never opens, so Kubernetes never routes traffic to an unhealthy backend; the chart's default probes poll /_readiness every 5s (readiness), /_liveness every 10s (liveness), and allow up to 60 attempts at 2s intervals (startup) before Kubernetes gives up on the container starting.

Recovery from a lost hosted deployment is enumerated by the chart's own backup list: the relay private key (identity -- rotating it changes what federation peers recognize), the PostgreSQL database (the canonical event store), the S3 bucket (media blobs), the git PersistentVolumeClaim (on-disk pack-cache/working-tree state for the relay's git endpoint), and the owner's private key, held by the operator and not by the chart, restored by reinstalling with the same ownerPubkey.

Schema migrations run automatically at relay startup by default (BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE, default true) through an embedded sqlx::migrate! call, made race-safe across multiple replicas by a Postgres advisory lock; an operator may instead decouple migrations (migrate.autoMigrate=false) and run them out-of-band, but the chart's readiness probes check only DB connectivity, not schema freshness -- so a pod can appear healthy while serving against an unmigrated schema in that mode.

An optional HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales the relay Deployment on the larger recommendation from CPU utilization or average active WebSocket connections per pod (both knobs default off), and an optional PodDisruptionBudget only renders once the effective minimum replica count exceeds 1 -- both are chart-provided failure/recovery levers rather than defaults an operator gets for free.

Issue #669's category-specific Definition of Done requires this node to name the environment/topology and execution nodes, map Buzz containers/services/data stores to them, describe network/persistence/trust boundaries without exposing secrets, and link deployment automation/config as authority while documenting failure/recovery implications.

# Buzz on Kubernetes: deployment topology

## Scope

This node documents the **Kubernetes deployment topology for the Buzz relay**, as
declared by the chart at `deploy/charts/buzz/` — its execution nodes, the mapping
of Buzz's containers/services/data stores onto them, its network, persistence and
trust boundaries, and its failure/recovery implications. It is a description of
what the chart *declares*, cross-checked against the values and templates that
render it — not a report on a live cluster.

**Two deployment layers, not one — an ambiguity this issue's Definition of Done
does not resolve.** "The Kubernetes deployment" for Buzz names two different
things depending on who is asking:

1. **The chart itself** (`deploy/charts/buzz/`) — OSS, versioned independently via
   `chart-v*` tags, published to `oci://ghcr.io/block/buzz/charts/buzz`. This is
   what any self-hoster, and this document, can actually inspect.
2. **Block's staging cluster**, provisioned by the private
   `squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks` repository (Terraform + ArgoCD) — see
   [AGENTS.md's ecosystem table](../../../../../AGENTS.md#ecosystem). That repository
   is not present in this checkout. This node cannot verify its actual topology,
   values overrides, or network posture; it can only describe the chart that
   pipeline consumes as input, and says so explicitly rather than guessing at the
   private layer.

**The launchpad-26 fork does not operate a Kubernetes deployment at all.** The
fork's own hosted deployment (`launchpad/deploy/`) runs on a single VPS via
Docker Compose, guarded by `launchpad/deploy/run.sh` to pin an immutable
`ghcr.io/launchpad-26/buzz` image. It is a separate deployment concern from this
node and is not described further here.

## Topology and execution nodes

A chart release targets one Kubernetes namespace. Within it, the chart can
render up to five kinds of workload, each an independent execution node:

| Workload | Kind | Cardinality | Enabled by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relay | `Deployment` | `replicaCount` (or HPA-managed) | always |
| Device pairing relay | `Deployment` | `pairingRelay.replicaCount` | `pairingRelay.enabled` |
| In-cluster PostgreSQL | subchart | 1 (eval) | `postgresql.enabled` |
| In-cluster Redis | subchart | 1 (eval) | `redis.enabled` |
| In-cluster MinIO | `Deployment` | 1 (eval, `strategy: Recreate`) | `minio.enabled` |

The three bundled data-store workloads exist only in the **quickstart** profile
and are explicitly documented as eval-only, single-replica, non-HA. In the
**production** profile none of them render; PostgreSQL, Redis, and
S3-compatible storage are external managed services or self-hosted nodes
reached over the network, addressed by `externalPostgresql.url`,
`externalRedis.url`, and `s3.endpoint` respectively.

## Container/service/data-store mapping

- **Relay container** (`relay`, in the relay `Deployment`) — the single binary
  serving WebSocket, REST, and the web UI on the `app` port (3000), plus
  separate `health` and `metrics` ports. The chart's `Service` republishes all
  three ports under matching names, and an optional `Ingress` or `HTTPRoute`
  (mutually independent, either or neither may be enabled) fronts the `app`
  port for external clients.
- **Pairing relay container** (`pairing-relay`, its own `Deployment`+`Service`)
  — the stateless `buzz-pair-relay` binary from the same image, on its own
  WebSocket port. It advertises its URL in the main relay's NIP-11 document,
  but has no chart-managed `Ingress`/`HTTPRoute` of its own.
- **wait-for-bucket init container** — quickstart-only; blocks relay
  container start until the bundled MinIO bucket exists, avoiding a
  CrashLoopBackOff race against the relay's startup-fatal S3 conformance
  probe.
- **PostgreSQL** — canonical event store. External managed service in
  production; an in-cluster subchart Deployment in quickstart.
- **Redis** — backs `buzz-pubsub` fan-out. **Hard-required** whenever the
  effective minimum replica count exceeds 1; the chart **template-fails**
  rather than silently degrading if that invariant is violated.
- **S3-compatible object storage** — media blobs and Git objects/refs. Git
  state is object-store-backed per request (an ephemeral repo is hydrated from
  storage), with writer serialization via the object-store pointer CAS and
  repo-name uniqueness enforced in Postgres — so no shared/`ReadWriteMany`
  filesystem is required across replicas.
- **Git PersistentVolumeClaim** — one `ReadWriteOnce` PVC (or operator-supplied
  `existingClaim`, or an ephemeral `emptyDir` when persistence is disabled) is
  mounted **per relay replica**, holding that replica's local working copy of
  git repo state. It is not shared storage.

## Network boundaries

- **North-south entry**: an optional `Ingress` (`networking.k8s.io/v1`) or an
  optional `HTTPRoute` (Gateway API, `gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`) can front
  the relay `Service`. Neither is required — a platform may route to the
  `ClusterIP`/`LoadBalancer` `Service` directly, or the pairing-relay `Service`,
  by its own means.
- **East-west / cluster-internal**: the relay reaches Postgres, Redis, and
  object storage over whatever network path those endpoints are configured
  with (in-cluster `Service` DNS in quickstart; external URLs in production).
  The chart does not declare or constrain that path beyond the URL/endpoint
  values an operator supplies.
- **No NetworkPolicy is rendered by this chart.** No `networkpolicy.yaml`
  template exists under `deploy/charts/buzz/templates`, unlike the sibling
  `deploy/charts/buzz-push-gateway` chart, which does define one. Segmentation
  is left to the cluster's CNI, platform-level policy, or an operator-supplied
  `extraManifests` entry.

## Persistence boundaries

Per the Backups list below, the durable state an operator must protect spans
three different kinds of storage, each with a different Kubernetes-visible
shape: a Kubernetes `Secret` value (relay private key), an external database
(PostgreSQL), an external object store (S3-compatible), and a `PersistentVolumeClaim`
per replica (git working state). None of these are backed up by the chart
itself — it declares the resources and mounts, not a backup mechanism.

## Trust boundaries and secrets handling

- The relay Pod runs as a **dedicated, non-root identity**: fixed UID/GID
  `65532`, `runAsNonRoot: true`, `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault` at the Pod
  level, and `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` with **all Linux capabilities
  dropped** at the container level. `readOnlyRootFilesystem` is deliberately
  `false` — the relay's git path needs a writable working directory — which is
  a real, intentional narrowing of an otherwise hardened default, not an
  oversight.
- A dedicated `ServiceAccount` is created per release (when
  `serviceAccount.create` is true); no cluster-scoped RBAC is granted by this
  chart.
- **Two mutually exclusive secret paths.** `secrets.existingSecret` names a
  pre-created `Secret` (schema in `examples/secret-sample.yaml`) that
  production/GitOps deploys **must** use. Absent that, the chart renders its
  own `Secret` (`templates/secret-chart.yaml`) that autogenerates a relay
  private key, a git-hook HMAC secret, and any in-cluster DB/Redis/MinIO
  credentials via `randAlphaNum`, persisting them across upgrades through a
  Helm `lookup` against the existing `Secret`. **That path is explicitly
  documented as unsafe under GitOps**: ArgoCD and Flux render with
  `helm template`, under which `lookup` always returns empty, so every sync
  would mint fresh random secrets. No secret *values* are reproduced in this
  node — only the mechanism and its safe/unsafe boundary.
- The two committed GitOps examples — `examples/argocd-app.yaml` (ArgoCD
  `Application`, chart pulled as an OCI artifact) and
  `examples/flux-helmrelease.yaml` (Flux v2 `HelmRelease`) — are the
  authoritative reference for how `secrets.existingSecret` is wired into a
  production install; this node does not restate their content.

## Deployment automation as authority

This node is a description layer over automation that already exists and is
authoritative in its own right:

- `deploy/charts/buzz/README.md`, `Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, and
  `values.schema.json` — the chart's own documented and schema-validated
  contract.
- `deploy/charts/buzz/examples/argocd-app.yaml` and
  `examples/flux-helmrelease.yaml` — the canonical GitOps install shapes.
- `deploy/charts/buzz/examples/secret-sample.yaml` — the `existingSecret`
  schema.
- `.github/workflows/helm-chart.yml` (referenced by the README) — lints,
  unit-tests, and render-checks every PR/`main` change, and publishes the
  chart to GHCR only on a `chart-v*` tag.

Where this node and any of those disagree, they win — this is a description,
not a second copy of the contract.

## Failure and recovery implications

- **Unrecoverable-loss inventory** (from the chart README's Backups section):
  the `BUZZ_RELAY_PRIVATE_KEY` (rotating it changes relay identity — federation
  peers stop recognizing it), the PostgreSQL database (canonical event store),
  the S3 bucket (media blobs), the git `PersistentVolumeClaim` (on-disk repo
  state), and the operator's own owner private key (held outside the chart
  entirely; recovered by reinstalling with the same `ownerPubkey`).
- **Migrations and startup**: schema migrations run automatically at relay
  startup by default (`BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE=true`), serialized across replicas by
  a Postgres advisory lock. If an operator disables that
  (`migrate.autoMigrate=false`), the chart does **not** run migrations for
  them — the operator must run `buzz-admin migrate` before every
  install/upgrade. This matters for failure detection because the readiness
  probe checks DB *connectivity* only, not schema freshness: a pod can report
  ready against an unmigrated schema and only fail once real traffic hits it.
- **Rolling updates**: `RollingUpdate` with `maxSurge: 1`, `maxUnavailable: 0`
  — capacity never drops during a deploy. On `SIGTERM` the relay closes every
  live WebSocket with a `1012 Service Restart` frame; `drainJitterMs` (0 by
  default) can spread those closes to avoid a reconnect stampede against the
  database pool, bounded under the default 60s
  `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.
  Every replica is single-pod-scoped for one feature: `huddleAudioAvailable`
  defaults to disabled automatically once `replicaCount > 1`, because huddle
  audio is only documented as safe for single-pod relay deployments until an
  SFU exists.
- **Disruption and scaling are opt-in, not automatic**: a `PodDisruptionBudget`
  only renders when `podDisruptionBudget.enabled` is true *and* the effective
  minimum replica count exceeds 1. The optional HPA scales on the larger of
  CPU utilization or an average-active-WebSockets custom metric — CPU scaling
  needs a cluster Metrics Server, and the WebSocket metric additionally needs a
  custom-metrics adapter (for example, Prometheus Adapter); the chart creates
  the `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` object but does not install either
  prerequisite.
- **Extension surface**: init containers, volumes, relay volume mounts, and
  image command/args can be overridden through narrow chart values without
  forking the chart; `extraManifests` can add independent cluster resources
  but cannot modify the chart-owned relay `Deployment`. The chart does not
  validate cross-field correctness of these raw fragments — an operator who
  misconfigures an extension can still break their own release.

## Scope and omissions

**Out of scope, and not folded into this node:**

- **`buzz-backend-kubernetes`** (`crates/buzz-backend-kubernetes/`) — a
  Kubernetes backend *provider* that lets Buzz's agent harness launch remote
  coding agents as their own pods. This is a compute-provisioning concern for
  agent workloads, not the relay's own deployment topology, and is a distinct
  idea per `launchpad/docs/corpus/AGENTS.md`'s one-node-one-idea rule. It
  belongs in its own node.
- **`deploy/charts/buzz-push-gateway`** — a separate, optional chart for push
  notifications. Named here only as a pointer (and as the source of the
  NetworkPolicy contrast above), not documented in depth.
- **Block's actual staging-cluster configuration** — provisioned by the
  private `squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks` repository, not present in this
  checkout. This node describes the OSS chart that pipeline consumes; it does
  not describe the pipeline's Terraform, its ArgoCD `Application` values
  overrides, or the staging cluster's real network/RBAC posture. The one claim
  this node makes about that relationship (that staging most likely runs the
  chart's production profile, not quickstart) is recorded as an `INFERENCE`
  with confidence 0.6, not a `FACT`.
- **`values.schema.json`'s full field-by-field contract** and **`templates/_validate.tpl`'s
  exact fail-fast messages** — linked as authority above rather than restated,
  per this corpus's own guidance against duplicating a schema in prose.

**Expected but not verified when this node was written:**

- No live cluster (staging or otherwise) was inspected — every claim above is
  about what the chart *declares*, not about a running deployment's actual
  state, resource usage, or incident history.
- `helm template` / `helm unittest` were not run as part of authoring this
  node; the templates were read directly rather than rendered.

Back to the corpus root: [`launchpad/docs/corpus/README.md`](../../README.md).

evidence.statement: This node was authored and checked against repository revision a44cf52fc740ebebbdd671427480d14f0bce0115.

The repository's canonical Kubernetes deployment automation for Buzz is the Helm chart at deploy/charts/buzz, which deploys a single relay binary serving WebSocket, REST, and the web UI, backed by PostgreSQL, Redis, and S3-compatible object storage.

The chart has two operating profiles selected by values: production (default, external managed Postgres/Redis/S3, secrets.existingSecret, HA-capable) and quickstart (eval-only, in-cluster Postgres+Redis+MinIO subcharts/Deployments, chart-autogenerated secrets, single replica).

squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks is a separate, private repository that provisions Terraform + ArgoCD to deploy the relay's Helm chart to Block's staging Kubernetes cluster; this checkout does not contain that repository's manifests, so this node cannot verify the staging cluster's actual topology beyond what the OSS chart it consumes declares.

The launchpad-26 fork's own operated deployment (documented in launchpad/deploy/) targets a single VPS via Docker Compose, not Kubernetes; the Kubernetes chart documented here is upstream/OSS deployment automation that the fork does not itself operate.

The relay Pod template (deploy/charts/buzz/templates/deployment.yaml) is a single apps/v1 Deployment named via the chart's fullname helper, running one 'relay' container plus, only when the quickstart MinIO subchart is enabled, a 'wait-for-bucket' init container that blocks relay start until the MinIO bucket exists.

The relay container exposes three named container ports: app (3000, WebSocket+REST+web UI), health (configurable via service.healthPort), and metrics (configurable via service.metricsPort); the chart's Service (templates/service.yaml) republishes all three under the same names.

Optional ingress.enabled renders a networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress and optional httproute.enabled renders a gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 HTTPRoute; both are alternative north-south entry points in front of the same Service, and neither is required — a platform can also route to the Service directly.

pairingRelay.enabled renders a second, independent Deployment and Service running the same relay image with the buzz-pair-relay entrypoint on its own websocket port; the chart does not create an Ingress/HTTPRoute for it, so routing its public hostname is left to the operator's own platform ingress configuration.

Data-store mapping: PostgreSQL is the canonical event store, Redis backs buzz-pubsub fan-out and is hard-required by the chart whenever replicaCount (or the HPA's effective replica count) exceeds 1, and S3-compatible object storage holds media blobs and Git objects/refs (the git endpoint hydrates an ephemeral repo per request from object storage, so no ReadWriteMany filesystem is needed).

A PersistentVolumeClaim (templates/pvc-git.yaml, ReadWriteOnce by default) is created per release when persistence.git.enabled is true and no existingClaim is given; each relay replica mounts its own claim (or an ephemeral emptyDir when persistence is disabled), so this volume is not shared across replicas.

In production profile, external Postgres/Redis/S3 are physical or managed-service execution nodes outside the Kubernetes cluster, reached over the network from the relay Pod; in quickstart profile, Postgres, Redis, and MinIO instead run as additional in-cluster Deployments/subcharts (single replica, no HA) created by the same chart release.

evidence.statement: The chart does not create any NetworkPolicy resource for the relay or pairing-relay Deployments; no networkpolicy.yaml template exists under deploy/charts/buzz/templates, unlike the sibling deploy/charts/buzz-push-gateway chart, which does define one. Network segmentation for this chart is left to the cluster's CNI, an operator-supplied extraManifests entry, or platform-level policy.

Trust/identity boundary: the relay Pod runs under a dedicated ServiceAccount (created when serviceAccount.create is true), a Pod-level securityContext (runAsNonRoot, fixed non-root UID/GID 65532, RuntimeDefault seccomp) and a container-level securityContext (allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, all Linux capabilities dropped); readOnlyRootFilesystem is deliberately false because the relay's git path needs a writable working directory.

Secrets handling: production/GitOps deploys must set secrets.existingSecret to a pre-created Secret (schema documented in examples/secret-sample.yaml); the chart's own templates/secret-chart.yaml (autogenerated relay private key, git-hook HMAC, and in-cluster DB/Redis/MinIO credentials via randAlphaNum, persisted across upgrades through a Secret lookup) is explicitly documented as unsafe for GitOps because ArgoCD/Flux render with helm template, under which Helm's lookup returns empty and every sync would regenerate fresh random secrets.

Two committed GitOps examples name the actual deployment automation an operator or reviewer should treat as authoritative for production topology: examples/argocd-app.yaml (an ArgoCD Application pulling the chart as an OCI artifact from oci://ghcr.io/block/buzz/charts/buzz) and examples/flux-helmrelease.yaml (a Flux v2 HelmRelease).

Failure/recovery: the README's Backups section names five things whose loss is unrecoverable data loss for a given deployment — the relay private key (rotation changes relay identity, breaking federation-peer recognition), the PostgreSQL database (canonical event store), the S3 bucket (media blobs), the Git PVC (on-disk repo state served by the relay's git endpoint), and the operator's own owner private key (held outside the chart entirely).

Schema migrations run automatically at relay startup (BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE, default true) using a Postgres advisory lock so multiple replicas can start concurrently without racing; if an operator instead sets migrate.autoMigrate=false, the chart does not run migrations at all and the operator must run buzz-admin migrate before every install/upgrade, because the readiness probe checks DB connectivity only, not schema freshness, so an unmigrated pod can pass readiness and fail under load.

Rolling updates use a RollingUpdate strategy with maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0 (no capacity drop during a deploy); on SIGTERM the relay closes every live WebSocket with a 1012 Service Restart frame, and an optional drainJitterMs spreads those closes over a per-socket random delay to avoid a reconnect stampede against the database pool, bounded under the default 60s terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

Optional recovery/availability controls exist but are opt-in and off by default: a PodDisruptionBudget template only renders when podDisruptionBudget.enabled is true and the effective minimum replica count exceeds 1, and an HPA (autoscaling.enabled) scales on the larger of CPU utilization or an average-active-WebSockets custom metric, requiring a cluster Metrics Server (and, for the websocket metric, a custom-metrics adapter) that the chart itself does not install.

Extending the chart-managed relay Deployment (init containers, volumes, relay volume mounts, command/args overrides) is done through narrow, documented extension values rather than a Helm chart fork; extraManifests can add independent cluster resources but cannot modify the chart-owned relay Deployment itself.

buzz-backend-kubernetes is a separate crate — a Kubernetes backend provider that lets Buzz's agent harness launch remote coding agents as their own pods — and is a distinct compute-provisioning concern from the relay's own deployment topology documented in this node, so it is deliberately out of scope here rather than folded in.

Because the private squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks pipeline's actual Terraform/ArgoCD manifests were not inspected, it is a reasonable but unverified inference that Block's staging cluster deployment follows this chart's production profile (external managed Postgres/Redis/S3, secrets.existingSecret) rather than the quickstart profile, since the quickstart profile is explicitly documented as eval-only and not GitOps-safe.

body:
# Local development deployment

The canonical description of Buzz's **local development** environment/topology: what
runs where, how the pieces map to each other, the network and persistence boundaries
between them, and what to do when a piece fails. Scoped to local development only —
staging and production topology (Kubernetes via `block-coder-tf-stacks`, the relay
Docker image built by `sprout-oss`) is a separate concern and not covered here.

## Environment / topology

Local development is **single-node**: one developer machine hosts every component.
There is no multi-host topology to diagram — the "nodes" that matter here are the
*processes and containers on that one machine*, not physical or virtual hosts. Two
kinds of execution unit exist side by side:

- **Docker containers**, orchestrated by `docker-compose.yml` and started via
  `docker compose up -d` (wrapped by the Justfile's `_ensure-services` recipe).
- **Native host processes**: the Rust relay/admin binaries (`cargo run -p buzz-relay`,
  `cargo run -p buzz-admin`), the Tauri desktop app, and the Vite dev server for the
  web client — none of these are containerized in local dev.

## Containers, services, and data stores

`docker-compose.yml` defines six services, all on one bridge network (`buzz-net`):

| Service | Image | Purpose | Persistence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `postgres` | `postgres:17-alpine` | primary relational store | volume `buzz-postgres-data` |
| `redis` | `redis:7-alpine` | pub/sub fan-out, presence, typing indicators | none — ephemeral |
| `adminer` | `adminer:latest` | Postgres browser UI, depends on `postgres` healthy | n/a |
| `keycloak` | `quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.0` | local OAuth/OIDC testing | none — `dev-mem` DB |
| `minio` | `minio/minio:latest` | S3-compatible object store (media, git CAS) | volume `buzz-minio-data` |
| `minio-init` | `minio/mc:latest` | one-shot: creates `buzz-media` bucket, sets it private | n/a, exits after run |
| `prometheus` | `prom/prometheus:latest` | scrapes relay metrics | volume `buzz-prometheus-data` |

Alongside these, the native host processes connect to the containers over
`localhost`:

- **`buzz-relay`** (`cargo run -p buzz-relay`, or `just relay` / `just dev`) —
  connects to `postgres` (`DATABASE_URL`) and `redis` (`REDIS_URL`), and to `minio`
  for media/S3 storage (`BUZZ_S3_ENDPOINT`).
- **`buzz-admin`** (`cargo run -p buzz-admin -- migrate`) — applies
  `migrations/*.sql` directly against Postgres; run by the `_ensure-migrations`
  Justfile recipe, not by the relay process itself (see *Persistence and migrations*
  below).
- **Desktop app** (Tauri) and **web client** (Vite) — connect to the relay over
  `ws://localhost:3000` / `http://localhost:3000`, not to the containers directly.

`buzz-search` (Postgres full-text search) has no separate container — it runs inside
the `postgres` service. Note: `.env.example` documents `TYPESENSE_API_KEY` /
`TYPESENSE_URL`, and CONTRIBUTING.md's port table lists Typesense at
`localhost:8108`, but no `typesense` service exists in `docker-compose.yml`. That is
a real inconsistency between the environment template/docs and the actual compose
file, recorded as a gap below rather than resolved by guessing which is stale.

## Network boundaries

Every `docker-compose.yml` port publish is bound to `127.0.0.1` explicitly (for
example `127.0.0.1:5432:5432`), so none of the six Docker services in the table above
is reachable from another host on the network by default — they are local-loopback
only.

`buzz-relay` itself is different: its bind address defaults to `0.0.0.0:3000`
(`BUZZ_BIND_ADDR` unset), which listens on every network interface, not just
loopback. Its health port (default `8080`, `BUZZ_HEALTH_PORT`) and metrics port
(default `9102`, `BUZZ_METRICS_PORT`) follow the relay process's own bind behavior —
compose defines no publish rule for them because they are not containerized. So the
one process meant to be reached by real clients (desktop, web, mobile, other relays)
has a wider default network surface in local dev than the infrastructure it depends
on. A developer running local dev on a shared or untrusted network should be aware
the relay is not loopback-restricted by default the way Postgres/Redis/MinIO are.

`just dev` includes a port-conflict guard: before launching the desktop app it checks
whether the relay, health, or metrics port is already bound by another process (via
`lsof`) and refuses to launch against a possibly-stale relay, printing the offending
process instead.

## Persistence and migrations

Three of the six Docker services persist data across restarts via named volumes:
`buzz-postgres-data`, `buzz-minio-data`, `buzz-prometheus-data`. Redis has no volume
— both `docker-compose.yml` and `scripts/dev-reset.sh`'s own comment agree its data
is ephemeral and wiped on any container recreation.

**Migrations are applied explicitly, not automatically, in the local-dev flow
described here.** The Justfile's `_ensure-migrations` recipe runs
`cargo run -p buzz-admin -- migrate` (then seeds a local community) once Postgres and
Redis report healthy — this is what `just relay`, `just dev`, and `just setup` all
depend on. Separately, `buzz-relay`'s own startup code only applies migrations
itself when the `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE` environment variable is set truthy; it is unset
by default, so the relay process does not self-migrate on `just relay` / `just dev`.
The top-level `AGENTS.md` repo map describes `migrations/` as "auto-applied on relay
startup" — that is the deployed/production framing (where `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE` is
presumably set); the mechanism that actually runs migrations in the local-dev flow
this node documents is the explicit `buzz-admin migrate` step above, not relay
self-migration. `migrations/` holds 31 numbered SQL files today
(`0001_initial_schema.sql` through beyond `0020_join_policy_acceptances.sql`),
applied in order.

## Trust boundaries (without exposing secrets)

Postgres, MinIO, and Keycloak in `docker-compose.yml` and `.env.example` use fixed,
non-secret placeholder credentials scoped to the local-only (`127.0.0.1`) network
described above. This document does not restate those values — `docker-compose.yml`
and `.env.example` are the authoritative, already-committed source for them, and
duplicating them here would be a second copy that can drift.

`minio-init` sets the `buzz-media` bucket's anonymous access policy to `none`
(private) immediately after creating it, so the object store is not publicly
readable even within the local Docker network by default. `keycloak` runs in
`start-dev` / `dev-mem` mode — a non-persistent, development-only identity provider
for exercising OAuth/OIDC flows locally, not a boundary meant to resemble production
auth infrastructure.

## Deployment automation and configuration (authority)

This node describes the automation; it is not a substitute for reading it. The
authoritative sources are:

- [`Justfile`](../../../../../Justfile) — `bootstrap`, `setup`, `relay`, `relay-web`,
  `dev`, `down`, `reset`, `ps`, `logs`, and the internal `_ensure-services` /
  `_ensure-migrations` recipes.
- [`docker-compose.yml`](../../../../../docker-compose.yml) — the six-service
  topology in the table above.
- [`.env.example`](../../../../../.env.example) — every environment variable local
  dev reads, with defaults and comments.
- [`scripts/dev-setup.sh`](../../../../../scripts/dev-setup.sh) — first-time and
  re-run setup: legacy `sprout`→`buzz` rename, service health-wait, migrations,
  desktop/web dependency install, git hook install.
- [`scripts/dev-reset.sh`](../../../../../scripts/dev-reset.sh) — full teardown:
  desktop dev state, then `docker compose down -v --remove-orphans` (deletes all
  three named volumes), then re-runs `dev-setup.sh`.
- [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../../../../../CONTRIBUTING.md) §"Setting Up the Development
  Environment" — prerequisites and the narrative walkthrough of the same commands.

## Failure and recovery implications

- **A Docker service fails to become healthy.** `_ensure-services` polls
  `docker inspect` health status for `buzz-postgres` and `buzz-redis` for up to 40
  attempts (~3s apart, ~120s total) before the recipe exits 1. Any recipe depending
  on `_ensure-migrations` (`just relay`, `just dev`, `just setup`) fails at that
  point rather than proceeding against unhealthy infrastructure.
- **The relay port is already in use.** `just dev`'s guard refuses to launch the
  desktop app against a possibly-stale relay and exits 1, naming the conflicting
  process rather than silently connecting to it.
- **Stop without losing data.** `just down` (`docker compose down`) stops containers
  and keeps all three named volumes intact.
- **Full recovery from corrupted/inconsistent local state.** `just reset`
  (`scripts/dev-reset.sh --yes`) is the only documented recovery path, and it is
  destructive: it deletes `buzz-postgres-data`, `buzz-minio-data`, and
  `buzz-prometheus-data` (Redis was already ephemeral) and recreates a clean
  environment from scratch via `dev-setup.sh`. Installed Buzz app state and its
  production keyring are explicitly preserved. There is no documented narrower
  recovery — for example, repairing a corrupted Postgres volume without discarding
  local dev data — in local-dev automation today; the only path this repository
  documents is full destructive reset.
- **Legacy state.** `dev-setup.sh` self-heals two categories of stale state
  automatically on every run: a legacy `sprout`-prefixed `DATABASE_URL`/`PGUSER`/
  `PGPASSWORD`/`PGDATABASE` in an existing `.env` is rewritten to the current `buzz`
  defaults, and any legacy `sprout-*`-named containers are stopped and removed so
  the current `buzz-*` containers can bind the same ports.

## Scope and omissions

**Out of scope for this node:** staging and production deployment topology
(Kubernetes via `block-coder-tf-stacks`, Terraform, ArgoCD, the relay Docker image
built by `sprout-oss`, Blox workstation agent provisioning via
`sprout-backend-blox`) — those are separate execution environments with their own
topology, owned by their respective repos per the top-level `AGENTS.md` ecosystem
table, and are not local development. Relay authentication/authorization internals,
event-kind design, and the desktop/mobile app architectures are covered by other
nodes, not this one.

**Gaps, named rather than resolved:**

- `.env.example` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s port table document a Typesense
  configuration block (`TYPESENSE_API_KEY`, `TYPESENSE_URL`, port `8108`) that has
  no corresponding service in `docker-compose.yml`, and the top-level `AGENTS.md`
  states search is Postgres full-text search (`buzz-search`), not Typesense. This
  reads as stale documentation rather than a hidden service, but that was not
  independently confirmed against Typesense-specific code, since no such code was
  found while gathering evidence for this node.
- Local-dev automation has no documented **non-destructive** recovery path for a
  corrupted or inconsistent Postgres volume — only the destructive `just reset`.
  Whether a narrower recovery (e.g. restoring the volume from a snapshot, or
  re-running only the migration step against existing data) is possible or intended
  was not established from the sources read for this node.
- This node's claims were verified by reading the cited files at the recorded

Local development runs every Buzz process and Docker service on a single developer machine; there is no separate host per component.
docker-compose.yml defines six services for local development: postgres, redis, adminer, keycloak, minio, minio-init, and prometheus.

Every docker-compose.yml service publishes its port bound to 127.0.0.1 only (e.g. postgres at 127.0.0.1:5432, redis at 127.0.0.1:6379), so none of the six Docker-hosted dev services is reachable from another host on the network by default.
buzz-relay's own bind address defaults to 0.0.0.0:3000 (BUZZ_BIND_ADDR unset), which listens on every network interface rather than only 127.0.0.1.

The relay's default bind address is therefore reachable from other hosts on the same network, unlike the Docker Compose infrastructure services, which are not — a wider default network surface for the one process meant to be reached by clients.

buzz-relay's health check port defaults to 8080 and its Prometheus metrics port defaults to 9102, both read from BUZZ_HEALTH_PORT and BUZZ_METRICS_PORT with no compose-defined publish rule, so their default bind follows the relay process's own bind behavior rather than compose's 127.0.0.1 convention.
`just relay` (relay: bootstrap _ensure-migrations) and `just dev` (dev: bootstrap _ensure-sidecar-stubs _ensure-migrations) both depend on _ensure-migrations, which depends on _ensure-services.
_ensure-services starts `docker compose up -d` and polls `docker inspect` health status for buzz-postgres and buzz-redis for up to 40 attempts (3s apart, ~120s) before failing the recipe.
_ensure-migrations runs `cargo run -p buzz-admin -- migrate` followed by scripts/seed-local-community.sh once services are healthy.

buzz-relay's own startup only applies database migrations when the BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE environment variable is truthy (true/1/yes/on, case-insensitive); it is unset by default, so relay startup alone does not migrate the database in the local-dev flow described above, which instead relies on the explicit buzz-admin migrate step run by _ensure-migrations.

The top-level AGENTS.md repo map describes migrations/ as "auto-applied on relay startup," which is the deployed/production framing; the local-dev path documented here (Justfile _ensure-migrations calling buzz-admin migrate explicitly) is the mechanism that actually applies them in this environment, and the two statements describe different points in the pipeline rather than contradicting each other. Recorded here because a reader coming from the top-level AGENTS.md would otherwise expect the relay process itself to migrate on `just relay` / `just dev`, which it does not unless BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE is explicitly set.
migrations/ contains 31 numbered SQL files (0001_initial_schema.sql through at least 0020_join_policy_acceptances.sql, continuing beyond it) applied in order by buzz-admin migrate.

docker-compose.yml declares three named volumes for persistence: buzz-postgres-data (postgres), buzz-minio-data (minio), and buzz-prometheus-data (prometheus); redis has no volume, so its data does not survive a container recreation.
scripts/dev-reset.sh's own comment states Redis data is ephemeral and always wiped on restart, matching the absence of a redis volume in docker-compose.yml.

`just down` (docker compose down) stops containers and preserves the three named volumes; `just reset` runs scripts/dev-reset.sh --yes, which runs `docker compose down -v --remove-orphans` (deleting all three volumes) and then re-execs dev-setup.sh to recreate a clean environment.

scripts/dev-reset.sh also runs scripts/reset-desktop-dev-state.sh before tearing down containers, and states that installed Buzz app state and its production keyring are preserved — only development-scoped desktop state and Docker volumes are wiped.
keycloak is provisioned in local dev for local OAuth/OIDC testing, per CONTRIBUTING.md's own description of what `just setup` starts.
adminer is a Postgres browser UI reachable at http://localhost:8082, and depends on postgres being healthy before starting.
minio-init runs once after minio is healthy, creates the buzz-media bucket if absent, and sets its anonymous access policy to none (private by default) before exiting.

Postgres, MinIO, and Keycloak dev credentials in docker-compose.yml and .env.example are fixed, non-secret placeholder values scoped to the local dev-only network (127.0.0.1) described above; this document does not restate them, since the compose file and .env.example are the authoritative, already-committed source.

.env.example documents a TYPESENSE_API_KEY and TYPESENSE_URL block, and CONTRIBUTING.md's port table lists Typesense at localhost:8108, but docker-compose.yml defines no typesense service and the top-level AGENTS.md states buzz-search performs Postgres full-text search rather than using Typesense.

`just dev` (the desktop-app dev recipe) refuses to launch when the relay, health, or metrics port is already bound by another process, printing which port and the offending process before exiting 1, rather than launching the desktop app against a stale relay.

First-time local setup is `just setup` (running `just bootstrap` first, then scripts/dev-setup.sh), which copies .env.example to .env if absent, starts and health-waits the Docker services, applies migrations, seeds a local community, and installs desktop and web JS dependencies.

scripts/dev-setup.sh renames a legacy `sprout`-named default DATABASE_URL/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD/PGDATABASE to the current `buzz` defaults for developers carrying over an older .env, and stops/removes any legacy `sprout-*`-named containers so the current `buzz-*` containers can bind the same ports.

body:
# Multi-community deployment

How one Buzz relay deployment serves many independent communities — the
execution nodes it runs on, which containers and data stores back it, the
network and trust boundary that keeps communities apart, and what deployment
automation governs it and recovers it from failure.

**Authoritative sources — this node duplicates none of their detail:**

| For | Read |
|---|---|
| How a request's community is resolved and why it fails closed | `crates/buzz-relay/src/tenant.rs` |
| The `communities` table and its lifecycle columns | `migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql`, `migrations/0016_community_archival.sql`, `migrations/0029_community_deletion.sql` |
| Operator-gated community creation | `crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/community_provisioning.rs` |
| Production/GitOps Kubernetes deployment, values, and profiles | `deploy/charts/buzz/README.md`, `deploy/charts/buzz/values.yaml` |
| Local development topology | `docker-compose.yml` |
| Listener layout and shutdown budget | `crates/buzz-relay/src/main.rs` (`serve`) |
| Cohort environments and their status | `launchpad/ENVIRONMENTS.md` |
| The wider Buzz ecosystem and which repo owns which pipeline | `AGENTS.md` (Ecosystem table) |
| A/B tenant-isolation conformance obligations | `docs/multi-tenant-conformance.md`, `crates/buzz-test-client/tests/conformance_multitenant.rs` |
| Git-on-object-storage design | `docs/git-on-object-storage.md` |

Where this document and any of those disagree, **they win**.

## Environment/topology and execution nodes

Three distinct execution-node shapes exist in this checkout today; the corpus's own
evidence entries above trace each claim.

1. **Local development — one developer's machine.** `docker-compose.yml` brings up
   seven containers on one bridge network (`buzz-net`): Postgres 17, Redis 7, Adminer,
   Keycloak (dev-mode), MinIO plus a one-shot `minio-init` bucket-provisioning job, and
   Prometheus. Every published port is bound to `127.0.0.1` only. The relay binary
   itself runs outside Compose (via `just relay` per the top-level `AGENTS.md`), against
   the Postgres and Redis containers.
2. **A Kubernetes cluster running the `deploy/charts/buzz` Helm chart** — one relay
   Deployment (`replicaCount`, default `1`), backed either by the chart's bundled
   in-cluster Postgres/Redis/MinIO (**quickstart** profile — single replica, no HA,
   eval-only) or by externally managed Postgres/Redis/S3-compatible storage
   (**production** profile — HA-capable at `replicaCount >= 2`, GitOps-renderable via
   ArgoCD or Flux). The chart optionally deploys a second, independent Deployment and
   Service for the device-pairing relay, using the same image.
3. **This cohort's staging Kubernetes cluster specifically** is provisioned and deployed
   by two repositories external to this checkout: `squareup/sprout-oss` builds the relay
   Docker image into an internal ECR, and `squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks` applies
   Terraform plus ArgoCD to deploy that image (via the Helm chart above) to the staging
   cluster. Neither repository is present in this checkout — see *Scope and omissions*.

`launchpad/ENVIRONMENTS.md` records that of the cohort's four named environments (local
development, a local VM harness, the shared cohort VPS, and contributors' machines),
only local development is `IMPLEMENTED` today; the others are `OPEN`. This node
describes the chart's designed topology for those environments, not a cohort
environment that is already standing on it end to end.

## Containers, services, and data stores mapped to execution nodes

| Component | Runs as | Data it owns / touches |
|---|---|---|
| `buzz-relay` (the relay binary) | One container/pod per replica; app router + optional pairing relay share the image but run as separate Deployments when the pairing relay is enabled | Reads/writes Postgres and Redis; reads/writes the S3-compatible bucket for media and git objects; optional local scratch volume for git working state |
| PostgreSQL | External managed service (production) or bundled subchart/container (quickstart, local dev) | The canonical event store, the `communities` table, all community-scoped tables (each carries `community_id`) |
| Redis | External managed service (production) or bundled subchart/container (quickstart, local dev) | `buzz-pubsub` cross-pod fan-out and presence/typing state; **required** whenever `replicaCount > 1` |
| S3-compatible object storage | External managed service (production) or bundled MinIO (quickstart, local dev) | Media blobs (Blossom) and git object/ref state (object-store-backed per request, not a shared filesystem — see `docs/git-on-object-storage.md`) |
| Device-pairing relay | Optional independent Deployment + Service, same image as `buzz-relay` | Stateless; advertised to clients via the main relay's NIP-11 document |
| Push gateway | Separate image (`Dockerfile.push-gateway`) and separate Helm chart (`deploy/charts/buzz-push-gateway`) | Out of this node's scope beyond noting it deploys independently of the main relay chart |
| Prometheus / metrics | Bundled container in local dev; `serviceMonitor` values hook in the chart for production scraping | Scrapes the relay's own metrics listener (below) |

## Network, persistence, and trust boundaries

**Community isolation is a Host-header trust boundary, enforced once, at connection
time — "row zero."** `bind_community` (`crates/buzz-relay/src/tenant.rs`) normalizes the
request's `Host` header and looks it up against the `communities` table's
`UNIQUE(lower(host))` index; an unmapped or empty host fails closed to a generic
rejection, with **no default-tenant fallback of any kind**. Server-internal call sites
that have no inbound `Host` header (git Smart-HTTP, the localhost pre-receive hook
callback, the workflow execution sink, startup tasks) resolve their own tenant through
the identical fail-closed path, keyed off the deployment's own configured `relay_url`
authority — never a shortcut around the seam. On the read path, a client-supplied
community claim (an event's `h` tag) is recorded only as a separate `claimed_community`
trace label; the community actually used for storage and fan-out is always the
host-resolved one (`crates/buzz-relay/src/conformance/mod.rs`).

**Community creation sits above the tenant boundary, not inside it.** Every other admin
action is authorized by looking up the caller's role within the resolved community
(`relay_members`); creating a community cannot be, because its effect is the creation of
tenancy itself. `POST /operator/communities` is instead gated by the deployment-level
`RELAY_OPERATOR_PUBKEYS` allowlist (empty by default — provisioning disabled), sits
outside the Nostr event ingest data plane, and is NIP-98-authenticated
(`crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/community_provisioning.rs`).

**Postgres write-fencing backs the boundary at the data layer for destructive
operations.** Whole-community deletion is a durable, lease/fence/checkpoint-guarded state
machine (`active -> quiescing -> fenced -> tombstone`) applied to every
community-scoped table in one atomic migration; the `communities` row itself is never
deleted, only tombstoned, so the unique host index and inbound references keep resolving
predictably (`migrations/0029_community_deletion.sql`). Archival is a lighter, separate
durable state (`archived_at`) under which a host stays reserved and continues to count
toward owner quotas (`migrations/0016_community_archival.sql`).

**Network surface.** The relay process binds four listeners: the app router on
`BUZZ_BIND_ADDR` (TCP, default `0.0.0.0:3000`), an optional app listener on a Unix domain
socket (`BUZZ_UDS_PATH`), a health-only TCP listener (`0.0.0.0:8080`), and a Prometheus
metrics TCP listener (`0.0.0.0:9102`) (`crates/buzz-relay/src/main.rs`). The chart's
`ingress`/`httproute` values are both disabled by default (`enabled: false`); an operator
supplies TLS termination and hostname routing externally when enabling either. Every
serving hostname must be seeded into `communities` before any client can reach it through
that hostname, and a deployment served without TLS additionally needs its `ws://` scheme
stated explicitly wherever shared, because the desktop client otherwise assumes `wss://`
for a scheme-less host (`launchpad/ENVIRONMENTS.md`).

**Persistence.** Git ref/object state served by the relay's git endpoint is
object-store-backed per request rather than filesystem-backed, and repo-name uniqueness
lives in Postgres — so horizontal scaling needs no shared `ReadWriteMany` volume. Each
pod's on-disk git working state is either a node-bound `ReadWriteOnce` PVC
(`persistence.git.enabled: true` — durable across pod restarts but not schedulable across
multiple nodes) or a per-pod `emptyDir` scratch volume (`persistence.git.enabled: false`),
which the chart's own values comments name as the correct choice for multi-replica HA,
because the object store and Postgres — not this disk — are the sources of truth
(`deploy/charts/buzz/values.yaml`).

**No secret values are reproduced in this node.** Env-var *names* that carry secrets
(`BUZZ_RELAY_PRIVATE_KEY`, `BUZZ_S3_ACCESS_KEY`, `BUZZ_S3_SECRET_KEY`, and the chart's
`secrets.existingSecret` keys) are named because the names themselves are the operable
contract; their values are never read or quoted here.

## Deployment automation and configuration as authority

- **Local development**: `docker-compose.yml` at the repo root is authoritative for the
  local container topology; `just setup` / `just relay` (top-level `AGENTS.md`) drive it.
- **The Kubernetes deployment shape**: `deploy/charts/buzz` (`values.yaml`,
  `values.schema.json`, `README.md`) is authoritative for both the quickstart and
  production profiles, published as an OCI artifact to
  `oci://ghcr.io/block/buzz/charts/buzz` by `.github/workflows/helm-chart.yml`, versioned
  independently of the relay image via its own `chart-v*` tags.
- **The push gateway's deployment shape**: `deploy/charts/buzz-push-gateway` is a
  separate chart with its own values and publish workflow
  (`.github/workflows/push-gateway-helm-chart.yml`), not covered further by this node.
- **This cohort's actual staging cluster**: per this repository's own `AGENTS.md`
  ecosystem table, `squareup/sprout-oss` builds and pushes the relay image and
  `squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks` applies Terraform plus ArgoCD to deploy it — but
  **both are private repositories not present in this checkout**, so their pipeline
  definitions are named, not opened; see *Scope and omissions*.

## Failure and recovery implications

- **Graceful shutdown is time-bounded and the chart's grace period is sized around it.**
  On `SIGTERM` the relay flips readiness to `503` immediately, waits a fixed `5s` before
  closing any listener (so Kubernetes stops routing new traffic first), then runs a
  `30s` hard-drain clock. A single WebSocket can stay open up to `35s` worst case, which
  fits inside the chart's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60` with headroom — but that
  headroom assumes no `preStop` hook adds further delay.
- **HA has one hard dependency: Redis.** `replicaCount > 1` requires a reachable Redis
  for `buzz-pubsub` fan-out across pods; the chart **fails template rendering outright**
  if that invariant is violated, rather than degrading silently at runtime.
- **Migrations run automatically and can mask readiness gaps.** Schema migrations are
  embedded in the relay binary and run at startup, gated by `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE` (default
  `true`) and serialized behind a Postgres advisory lock across replicas. Readiness
  probes verify only DB connectivity, not schema freshness — a pod can report healthy
  against an unmigrated schema and fail under load. Operators who disable
  `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE` own running `buzz-admin migrate` themselves before every
  install/upgrade.
- **A startup-fatal storage probe trades slow rollout for safety.** Object storage
  reachability is checked at startup whenever `BUZZ_GIT_CONFORMANCE_PROBE` is enabled
  (the relay default); failure there is startup-fatal, so a pod whose S3-compatible
  backend is unreachable never becomes ready in the first place, rather than serving
  degraded.
- **What to back up, and what is safe to lose.** The chart's own backup list is four
  items: `BUZZ_RELAY_PRIVATE_KEY` (the relay's federation identity — rotating it creates
  a new identity peers will not recognize), the PostgreSQL database (the canonical event
  store), the S3 bucket (media blobs, default bucket name `buzz-media`), and — only when
  `persistence.git.enabled: true` was chosen — the git PVC. In the recommended
  multi-replica configuration (`persistence.git.enabled: false`), the per-pod git scratch
  volume is deliberately *not* a backup concern: it is disposable, and the object store
  plus Postgres are what actually need protecting. The owner private key is held by the
  operator, not the chart, and is restored by re-installing with the same `ownerPubkey`.
- **Whole-community deletion is recoverable up to a point, and says so in its own state
  names.** The deletion state machine (`active -> quiescing -> fenced -> tombstone`) is
  lease/fence/checkpoint-guarded and never removes the `communities` row, so a request
  that fails partway leaves an inspectable, resumable state rather than a half-deleted
  tenant. Archival (`archived_at`) is the lighter-weight, non-destructive alternative for
  a community that should stop serving without triggering deletion.
- **Cross-community isolation is asserted by an executable test suite, but only when run
  deliberately.** `crates/buzz-test-client/tests/conformance_multitenant.rs` implements
  (not stubs) A/B isolation tests asserting no tenant-observable state crosses the
  community boundary, but every test is `#[ignore]`-gated by default because it needs a
  running relay with two live `Host` mappings against the same Postgres and Redis; it is
  selected explicitly with `--ignored` and two `RELAY_URL_*` environment variables. A CI
  run that does not pass `--ignored` exercises none of these tests.

## Scope and omissions

**This node covers** the shape of one Buzz relay deployment serving many communities:
its execution nodes, the containers and data stores mapped onto them, the network and
trust boundary that keeps communities apart, the configuration that is authoritative for
deploying it, and what is known about its failure and recovery behavior from this
checkout.

**This node does not cover, and these are gaps rather than silence:**

| Not covered here | Owned by |
|---|---|
| The push gateway's own deployment shape and failure modes | `deploy/charts/buzz-push-gateway` (a separate node, not yet written) |
| The actual (not merely named) content of `squareup/sprout-oss`'s CI pipeline and `squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks`'s Terraform/ArgoCD definitions | Those private repositories — not present in this checkout, so their pipeline definitions could not be opened; only their existence and role per this repo's `AGENTS.md` could be verified |
| Whether the cohort VPS or local VM harness environments in `launchpad/ENVIRONMENTS.md` are, at any given moment, actually running the topology this node describes | `launchpad/ENVIRONMENTS.md` — both are marked `OPEN`, not `IMPLEMENTED`, as of the revision this node was checked against |
| Per-type corpus template conformance for the `architecture`/deployment category | No per-type template exists yet in the merged corpus (per `launchpad/docs/corpus/AGENTS.md`); this node is written directly against `node.schema.json` and expects a later reshaping task |

**Expected but not verified when this node was written:**

- Whether `squareup/sprout-oss` and `squareup/block-coder-tf-stacks` deploy the exact
  chart and image this node describes, or a fork/variant of them, was not checked — those
  repositories are outside this checkout.
- Whether any environment in `launchpad/ENVIRONMENTS.md` marked `OPEN` has, since this
  node was written, moved to `IMPLEMENTED` was not re-checked at commit time; that
  document is the live source for its own status markers.
- No relationship edges are declared in this node's front matter. No other
  `architecture`/deployment node is merged in the corpus at the revision above to point
  at — `ls launchpad/docs/corpus/architecture/**/*.md` under `origin/launchpad` returns
  no result besides this file. The absence is deliberate, not an oversight; the first
  sibling node in this category is the moment to revisit it.
